newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Romanian president expects warm welcome in West.
newsitem.headline: Romanian president expects warm welcome in West.

text.p: Romania's new President Emil Constantinescu arrives in Brussels on Monday seeking to build on a sudden outpouring of support for renewed efforts to bring his country into the Western democratic club.

Constantinescu, on his first trip to the West since he triumphed over ex-communists in elections last November, will push Romania's case for swift membership of both the European Union and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO).
Western diplomats, impressed by his commitment to political and economic reforms, say he will receive a favourable hearing.
"Romania has come a long way in the last few months, it has completed its revolution and done it peacefully. There is a lot of support for Bucharest," said one western diplomatic source.

Constantinescu's first aim will be to secure financial backing from the European Union for a radical free-market reform package, including a privatisation drive promised by his centrist coalition government.
The package underpins loan talks with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. Both organisations withheld or suspended credits over the previous government's dismal reform record.

Romania already has an association agreement with the EU and is one of 10 former communist countries from central and eastern Europe clamouring for membership around the turn of the century, but faces a daunting economic challenge.

Inflation soared to 57 percent last year -- more than triple the target agreed with the IMF -- and the state budget gap is believed to have bulged to 5.7 percent of the gross domestic product (GDP) against a 2.2 percent forecast.

Until Constantinescu's election, Romania was seen as one of the countries least likely to win quick membership, its former communist leaders seen as paying only lip-service to required political and economic reforms.

That has all changed. In the last few weeks, a succession of Western politicians, keen to avoid a repeat of the instability now shaking Bulgaria, have visited Bucharest to express support for the government.

U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum was the latest to praise the new government in Bucharest, saying the country was now on the right path for membership of NATO and the other main Western institutions.
He told Reuters on Saturday after talks with Foreign Secretary Adrian Severin that the Cold War had kept Romania out of Europe's main stream.

"One of the United States' most important goals is to make sure that this main stream develops through the continent. It is very important that a country like the U.S. understand the debt we have to countries like Romania," he said.

"Romania and its people have shown a political maturity that bodes well for relations between Romania and the U.S. and for Romania's quest to enter into NATO and other Euro-Atlantic structures," a joint statement said after the talks.
NATO plans to name its first new members from former communist Europe at a summit in Madrid in July.
Romania, a long shot behind favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, has recently won powerful backing from France to be admitted in the first wave.
President Jacques Chirac, a strong support of both EU and NATO enlargement, is to visit Bucharest later this month.
Alliance diplomats say Italy and Greece are also backing Romania -- albeit more discreetly than Paris.
The alliance's military wing has been impressed by Romania's diligent efforts to bring its army -- the second largest among the applicant nations after Poland -- into line with NATO requirements.

"Romania is no longer a dark horse, it is a serious candidate. There is a lot of support for them. It (NATO membership) makes political, strategic, and even military sense -- on top of that they are great lobbyists," said one NATO source.
